newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hewlett-Packard says Asia PC sales on target.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard says Asia PC sales on target.

text.p: A senior official from Hewlett-Packard Co (HP) said on Monday its personal computer business will meet sales targets for the Asia-Pacific region this year despite a slowdown in some product lines.

"We will make the numbers that we have committed for Asia-Pacific this year," said Duane Zitzner, vice president and general manager of HP's personal information products group, in an interview with Reuters.
He declined to give details, except to add that Asia's performance was "within budget".
In the August announcement of its third quarter earnings, chief executive officer Lewis Platt voiced his concern over the slowdown in orders growth in the United States and Asia-Pacific.
But Zitzner was confident about PC growth prospects, especially in Asia.

In a news conference in India last month, HP said it expected revenue from Asia-Pacific PC sales to grow an average 35 percent a year over the next three years, from $1.8 billion in 1996 to $4.4 billion in 1999.
India, China and Indonesia were identified as target markets for investments and infrastructure.

HP on Monday quoted International Data Corp as reporting that HP beat Compaq and IBM to become the leading PC supplier in China in the second quarter, with 11.4 percent revenue share of China's PC market compared to 6.5 percent in the first quarter.
Despite a slowdown in the home PC line, Zitzner was upbeat about the commercial side of the business.
"I think competition has become fierce today because of a fair number of vendors. But the business is fine."
California-based HP said on Monday it had become the second largest supplier of corporate desktop PCs in the U.S.
The company said in a statement it had increased its unit shipments by 75 percent over the same period last year, giving it a 14.8 percent share of the U.S. corporate PC market.
Zitzner said HP continued to aim to be a systems company in the PC business, providing total solutions to meet customers' needs.

On whether he sees a need for HP to team up with software companies or buy into software firms, like IBM buying Lotus, Zitzner said: "We prefer to continue to work with the software people to ensure their products and ours will work well...You don't have to own them," he said.
He said HP spends about 10 percent of revenue on research and development to keep up with market needs.
